      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> C</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">HCV</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C?<p><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> is inflammation of the <span class="qt0">liver</span>. Inflammation is swelling that happens when tissues of the body are injured or infected. Inflammation can damage organs.</p><p>There are different types of <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>. One type, <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C, is caused by the <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C virus (HCV). <span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> C can range from a mild illness lasting a few weeks to a serious, lifelong illness.</p><p><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> C can be acute or chronic:</p><ul><li>Acute <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C is a short-term infection. The symptoms can last up to 6 months. Sometimes your body is able to fight off the infection and the virus goes away. But for most people, an acute infection leads to chronic infection.</li><li>Chronic <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C is a long-lasting infection. If it is not treated, it can last for a lifetime and cause serious health problems, including <span class="qt0">liver</span> damage, cirrhosis (scarring of the <span class="qt0">liver), <span class="qt2">liver</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, and even death.</li></ul>How is <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C spread?<p><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> C spreads through contact with the blood of someone who has HCV. This contact may be through:</p><ul><li>Sharing drug needles or other drug materials with someone who has HCV. In the United States, this is the most common way that people get <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C.</li><li>Getting an accidental stick with a needle that was used on someone who has HCV. This can happen in health care settings.</li><li>Being tattooed or pierced with tools or inks that were not sterilized after being used on someone who has HCV.</li><li>Having contact with the blood or open sores of someone who has HCV.</li><li>Sharing personal care items that may have come in contact with another person's blood, such as razors or toothbrushes.</li><li>Being born to a mother with HCV.</li><li>Having unprotected sex with someone who has HCV.</li></ul><p>Before 1992, <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C was also commonly spread through blood transfusions and organ transplants. Since then, there has been routine testing of the U.S. blood supply for HCV. It is now very rare for someone to get HCV this way.</p>Who is more likely to get <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C?<p>You are more likely to get <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C if you:</p><ul><li>Have injected drugs</li><li>Had a blood transfusion or organ transplant before July 1992</li><li>Have hemophilia and received clotting factor before 1987</li><li>Have been on kidney dialysis</li><li>Have been in contact with blood or infected needles at work</li><li>Have had tattoos or body piercings</li><li>Have worked or lived in a prison</li><li>Were born to a mother with <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C</li><li>Have HIV</li><li>Have had more than one sex partner in the last 6 months</li><li>Have had a sexually transmitted infection (STI)</li><li>Are a man who has had sex with men (MSM)</li></ul><p>If you are at high risk for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C, your health care provider will likely recommend that you get tested for it.</p>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C?<p>Most people with <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C have no symptoms. Some people with acute <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C do have symptoms within 1 to 3 months after they are exposed to the virus. These symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>Dark yellow urine</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Fever</li><li>Gray- or clay-colored stools</li><li>Joint pain</li><li>Loss of appetite</li><li>Nausea and/or vomiting</li><li>Pain in your abdomen (belly)</li><li>Jaundice (yellowish eyes and skin)</li></ul><p>If you have chronic <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C, you probably will not have symptoms until it causes complications. This can happen decades after you were infected. For this reason, <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C screening is important, even if you have no symptoms.</p>What other problems can <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C cause?<p>Without treatment, <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C may lead to cirrhosis, <span class="qt0">liver</span> failure, and <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">liver</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. Early diagnosis and treatment of <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C can prevent these complications.</p>How is <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C diagnosed?<p>Providers diagnose <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C based on your medical history, a physical exam, and blood tests.</p><p>If you do have <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C, you may need additional tests to check for <span class="qt0">liver</span> damage. These tests may include other blood tests, an ultrasound of the <span class="qt0">liver, and a liver</span> biopsy.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C?<p>Treatment for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C is with antiviral medicines. They can cure the disease in most cases.</p><p>If you have acute <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C, your provider may wait to see if your infection becomes chronic before starting treatment.</p><p>If your <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C causes cirrhosis, you should see a doctor who specializes in <span class="qt0">liver</span> diseases. Treatments for health problems related to cirrhosis include medicines, surgery, and other medical procedures. If your <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C leads to <span class="qt0">liver</span> failure or <span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">liver</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, you may need a <span class="qt0">liver</span> transplant.</p>Can <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C be prevented?<p>There is no vaccine for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C. But you can help protect yourself from <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C infection by:</p><ul><li>Not sharing drug needles or other drug materials.</li><li>Wearing gloves if you have to touch another person's blood or open sores.</li><li>Making sure your tattoo artist or body piercer uses sterile tools and unopened ink.</li><li>Not sharing personal items such toothbrushes, razors, or nail clippers.</li><li>Using a latex condom during sex. If your or your partner is allergic to latex, you can use polyurethane condoms.</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/hepatitisb.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> B</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">HBV</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>?<p><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> is inflammation of the <span class="qt0">liver</span>. Inflammation is swelling that happens when tissues of the body are injured or infected. It can damage your <span class="qt0">liver</span>. This swelling and damage can affect how well your <span class="qt0">liver</span> functions.</p>What is <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B?<p><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> B is a type of viral <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>. It can cause an acute (short-term) or chronic (long-term) infection. People with an acute infection usually get better on their own without treatment. Some people with chronic <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B will need treatment.</p><p>Thanks to a vaccine, <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B is not very common in the United States. It is more common in certain parts of the world, such as sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia.</p>What causes <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B?<p><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> B is caused by the <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B virus. The virus spreads through contact with blood, semen, or other body fluids from a person who has the virus.</p>Who is at risk for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B?<p>Anyone can get <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B, but the risk is higher in:</p><ul><li>Infants born to mothers who have <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B</li><li>People who inject drugs or share needles, syringes, and other types of drug equipment</li><li>Sex partners of people with <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B, especially if they are not using latex or polyurethane condoms during sex</li><li>Men who have sex with men</li><li>People who live with someone who has <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B, especially if they use the same razor, toothbrush, or nail clippers</li><li>Health care and public-safety workers who are exposed to blood on the job</li><li>Hemodialysis patients</li><li>People who have lived in or traveled often to parts of the world where <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B is common</li><li>People who have diabetes, <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C, or HIV</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B?<p>Often, people with <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B don't have symptoms. <span class="qt3">Adults</span> and children over 5 are more likely to have symptoms than younger children.</p><p>Some people with acute <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B have symptoms 2 to 5 months after infection. These symptoms can include:</p><ul><li>Dark yellow urine</li><li>Diarrhea</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Fever</li><li>Gray- or clay-colored stools</li><li>Joint pain</li><li>Loss of appetite</li><li>Nausea and/or vomiting</li><li>Abdominal pain</li><li>Yellowish eyes and skin, called jaundice</li></ul><p>If you have chronic <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B, you may not have symptoms until complications develop. This could be decades after you were infected. For this reason, <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B screening is important, even if you have no symptoms. Screening means that you are tested for a disease even though you don't have symptoms. If you are at high risk, your health care provider may suggest  screening.</p>What other problems can <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B cause?<p>In rare cases, acute <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B can cause <span class="qt0">liver</span> failure.</p><p>Chronic <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B can develop into a serious disease that causes long-term health problems such as cirrhosis (scarring of the <span class="qt0">liver), <span class="qt2">liver</span></span><span class="qt2"> </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span><span class="qt2">, and </span><span class="qt0"><span class="qt2">liver</span></span> failure.</p><p>If you have ever had <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B, the virus may become active again, or reactivated, later in life. This could start to damage the <span class="qt0">liver</span> and cause symptoms.</p>How is <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B diagnosed?<p>To diagnose <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B, your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis:</p><ul><li>A medical history, which includes asking about your symptoms</li><li>A physical exam</li><li>Blood tests, including tests for viral <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span></li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B?<p>If you have acute <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B, you probably don't need treatment. Some people with chronic <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B don't need treatment. But if you have a chronic infection and blood tests show that <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B could be damaging your <span class="qt0">liver</span>, you may need to take antiviral medicines.</p>Can <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B be prevented?<p>The best way to prevent <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B is to get the <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B vaccine.</p><p>You can also reduce your chance of <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B infection by:</p><ul><li>Not sharing drug needles or other drug materials</li><li>Wearing gloves if you have to touch another person's blood or open sores</li><li>Making sure your tattoo artist or body piercer uses sterile tools</li><li>Not sharing personal items, such as toothbrushes, razors, or nail clippers</li><li>Using a latex condom during sex. If your or your partner is allergic to latex, you can use polyurethane condoms.</li></ul><p>If you think you have been in contact with the <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B virus, see your health care provider right away. Your provider may give you a dose of the <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B vaccine to prevent infection. In some cases, your provider may also give you a medicine called <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B immune globulin (HBIG). You need to get the vaccine and the HBIG (if needed) as soon as possible after coming into contact with the virus. It is best if you can get them within 24 hours.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/alcohol.html">
      <content name="title">Alcohol</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Alcohol Consumption</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Binge Drinking</content>
      <content name="altTitle">College Drinking</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Drinking</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Many Americans drink alcohol at least occasionally. The  Dietary Guidelines for Americans say that <span class="qt3">adults</span> of legal drinking age should either not drink or drink in moderation. Drinking less is better for your health than drinking more. Also, there are some people who should not drink at all.</p><p>If you are going to drink, it's important to know how alcohol affects you and how much is too much.</p>How does alcohol affect the body?<p>Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant. This means that it is a drug that slows down brain activity. It can change your mood, behavior, and self-control. It can cause problems with memory and thinking clearly. Alcohol can also affect your coordination and physical control.</p><p>Alcohol also has effects on the other organs in your body. For example, it can raise your blood pressure and heart rate. If you drink too much at once, it could make you throw up.</p>Why are the effects of alcohol different from person to person?<p>Alcohol's effects vary from person to person, depending on a variety of factors, including:</p><ul><li>How much you drink</li><li>How often you drink</li><li>Your age</li><li>Your sex</li><li>Your genetics</li><li>Your overall health</li><li>Whether or not you have a family history of alcohol problems</li></ul>What is moderate drinking?<ul><li>For most women, moderate drinking is no more than 1 standard drink a day</li><li>For most men, moderate drinking is no more than 2 standard drinks a day</li></ul><p>Even though moderate drinking may be safe for many people, there are still risks. Moderate drinking can raise the risk of death from certain <span class="qt1">cancers</span> and heart diseases.</p>What is a standard drink?<p>In the United States, a standard drink is one that contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol, which is found in:</p><ul><li>12 ounces of regular beer (5% alcohol content)</li><li>5 ounces of wine (12% alcohol content)</li><li>1.5 ounces or a "shot" of distilled spirits or liquor (40% alcohol content)</li></ul>Who should not drink alcohol?<p>Some people should not drink alcohol at all, including those who:</p><ul><li>Are in recovery from an alcohol use disorder (AUD)</li><li> Are unable to control the amount they drink</li><li>Are under age 21</li><li>Are pregnant or trying to become pregnant</li><li>Are taking medicines that can interact with alcohol</li><li>Have medical conditions that can get worse if you drink alcohol</li><li>Are planning on driving</li><li>Will be operating machinery or doing activities that require skill, coordination, and alertness</li></ul><p>If you have questions about whether it is safe for you to drink, talk with your health care provider.</p>What is excessive drinking?<p>Excessive drinking includes binge drinking and heavy alcohol use:</p><ul><li>Binge drinking is drinking so much at once that your blood alcohol concentration (BAC) level is 0.08% or more: 
  <ul><li>For men, this usually happens after having 5 or more drinks within a few hours.</li><li>For women, it is usually after about 4 or more drinks within a few hours.</li></ul>
</li><li>Heavy alcohol use means:
  <ul><li>For men, having more than 5 drinks on any day or more than 15 drinks per week.</li><li>For women, having more than 4 drinks on any day or more than 8 drinks per week.</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>Binge drinking raises your risk of injuries, car crashes, and alcohol overdose. It also puts you at risk of becoming violent or being the victim of violence.</p><p>Heavy alcohol use over a long period of time may cause health problems such as:</p><ul><li>Alcohol use disorder (AUD)</li><li><span class="qt0">Liver</span> diseases, including cirrhosis and alcohol-associated <span class="qt0">liver</span> disease (ALD)</li><li>Heart diseases</li><li>Increased risk of certain <span class="qt1">cancers</span></li><li>Increased risk of injuries</li></ul><p>Heavy alcohol use can also cause problems at home, at work, and with friends. But treatment can help.</p><p>NIH: National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/acutelymphocyticleukemia.html">
      <content name="title">Acute Lymphocytic Leukemia</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">ALL</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Leukemia, Acute Lymphoblastic</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Leukemia, Acute Lymphocytic</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is leukemia?<p>Leukemia is a term for <span class="qt1">cancers</span> of the blood cells. Leukemia starts in blood-forming tissues such as the bone marrow. Your bone marrow makes the cells which will develop into white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. Each type of cell has a different job:</p><ul><li>White blood cells help your body fight infection</li><li>Red blood cells deliver oxygen from your lungs to your tissues and organs</li><li>Platelets help form clots to stop bleeding</li></ul><p>When you have leukemia, your bone marrow makes large numbers of abnormal cells. This problem most often happens with white blood cells. These abnormal cells build up in your bone marrow and blood. They crowd out the healthy blood cells and make it hard for your cells and blood to do their work.</p>What is acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL)?<p>Acute lymphocytic leukemia is a type of acute leukemia. It's also called ALL and acute lymphoblastic leukemia. "Acute" means that it usually gets worse quickly if it's not treated. ALL is the most common type of <span class="qt1">cancer</span> in children. It can also affect <span class="qt3">adults</span>.</p><p>In ALL, the bone marrow makes too many lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell. These cells normally help your body fight infection. But in ALL, they are abnormal and cannot fight infection very well. They also crowd out the healthy cells, which can lead to infection, anemia, and easy bleeding. These abnormal cells can also spread to other parts of the body, including the brain and spinal cord.</p>What causes acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL)?<p>ALL happens when there are changes in the genetic material (DNA) in bone marrow cells. The cause of these genetic changes is unknown. However, there are certain factors that raise your risk of ALL.</p>Who is at risk for acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL)?<p>The factors that raise your risk of ALL include:</p><ul><li>Being male</li><li>Being white</li><li>Being over age 70</li><li>Having had chemotherapy or radiation therapy</li><li>Having been exposed to high levels of radiation</li><li>Having certain genetic disorders, such as Down syndrome</li></ul>What are the symptoms of acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL)?<p>The signs and symptoms of ALL include:</p><ul><li>Weakness or feeling tired</li><li>Fever or night sweats</li><li>Easy bruising or bleeding</li><li>Petechiae, which are tiny red dots under the skin. They are caused by bleeding.</li><li>Shortness of breath</li><li>Weight loss or loss of appetite</li><li>Pain in the bones or stomach</li><li>Pain or feeling of fullness below the ribs</li><li>Swollen lymph nodes - you may notice them as painless lumps in the neck, underarm, stomach, or groin</li><li>Having had many infections</li></ul>How is acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider may use many tools to diagnose ALL and figure out which subtype you have:</p><ul><li>A physical exam</li><li>A medical history</li><li>Blood tests, such as
      <ul><li>Complete blood count (CBC) with differential</li><li>Blood chemistry tests such as a basic metabolic panel (BMP), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), kidney function tests, <span class="qt0">liver</span> function tests, and electrolyte panel</li><li>Blood smear</li></ul>  
</li><li>Bone marrow tests. There are two main types - bone marrow aspiration and bone marrow biopsy. Both tests involve removing a sample of bone marrow and bone. The samples are sent to a lab for testing.</li><li>Genetic tests to look for gene and chromosome changes</li></ul><p>If you are diagnosed with ALL, you may have additional tests to see whether the <span class="qt1">cancer</span> has spread. These include imaging tests and a lumbar puncture, which is a procedure to collect and test cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).</p>What are the treatments for acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL)?<p>Treatments for ALL include:</p><ul><li>Chemotherapy</li><li>Radiation therapy</li><li>Chemotherapy with stem cell transplant</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that attack specific <span class="qt1">cancer</span> cells with less harm to normal cells</li></ul><p>Treatment is usually done in two phases:</p><ul><li>The goal of the first phase is to kill the leukemia cells in the blood and bone marrow. This treatment puts the leukemia into remission. Remission means that the signs and symptoms of <span class="qt1">cancer</span> are reduced or have disappeared.</li><li>The second phase is known as post-remission therapy. Its goal is to prevent a relapse (return) of the <span class="qt1">cancer</span>. It involves killing any remaining leukemia cells that may not be active but could begin to regrow.</li></ul><p>Treatment during both phases also usually includes central nervous system (CNS) prophylaxis therapy. This therapy helps prevent the spread of leukemia cells to the brain and spinal cord. It may be high dose chemotherapy or chemotherapy injected into the spinal cord. It also sometimes includes radiation therapy.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt1">Cancer</span> Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/vitaminddeficiency.html">
      <content name="title">Vitamin D Deficiency</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Osteomalacia </content>
      <content name="altTitle">Hypovitaminosis D</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Low Vitamin D</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is vitamin D deficiency?<p>Vitamin D deficiency means that your body is not getting enough vitamin D to stay healthy.</p>Why do I need vitamin D and how do I get it?<p>Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium. Calcium is one of the main building blocks of bone. Vitamin D also has a role in your nervous, muscle, and immune systems.</p><p>You can get vitamin D in three ways: through your skin, from your diet, and from supplements. Your body forms vitamin D naturally after exposure to sunlight. But too much sun exposure can lead to skin aging and skin <span class="qt1">cancer</span>, so many people try to get their vitamin D from other sources.</p>How much vitamin D do I need?<p>The amount of vitamin D you need each day depends on your age.  The recommended amounts, in international units (IU), are:</p><ul><li>Birth to 12 months: 400 IU</li><li>Children 1-13 years: 600 IU</li><li>Teens 14-18 years: 600 IU</li><li><span class="qt3">Adults</span> 19-70 years: 600 IU</li><li><span class="qt3">Adults</span> 71 years and older: 800 IU</li><li>Pregnant and breastfeeding women: 600 IU</li></ul><p>People at high risk of vitamin D deficiency may need more. Check with your health care provider about how much you need.</p>What causes vitamin D deficiency?<p>You can become deficient in vitamin D for different reasons:</p><ul><li>You don't get enough vitamin D in your diet</li><li>You don't absorb enough vitamin D from food (a malabsorption problem)</li><li>You don't get enough exposure to sunlight</li><li>Your <span class="qt0">liver</span> or kidneys cannot convert vitamin D to its active form in the body</li><li>You take medicines that interfere with your body's ability to convert or absorb vitamin D</li></ul>Who is at risk of vitamin D deficiency?<p>Some people are at higher risk of vitamin D deficiency:</p><ul><li>Breastfed infants, because human milk is a poor source of vitamin D. If you are breastfeeding, give your infant a supplement of 400 IU of vitamin D every day.</li><li>Older <span class="qt3">adults</span>, because your skin doesn't make vitamin D when exposed to sunlight as efficiently as when you were young, and your kidneys are less able to convert vitamin D to its active form.</li><li>People with dark skin, which has less ability to produce vitamin D from the sun.</li><li>People with conditions that make it difficult to absorb nutrients from food, such as Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, and celiac disease.</li><li>People who have obesity, because their body fat binds to some vitamin D and prevents it from getting into the blood.</li><li>People who have had gastric bypass surgery, a type of weight loss surgery which creates a bypass of part of the small intestine. Since vitamin D is absorbed there, bypassing part of it makes it harder to absorb enough vitamin D. </li><li>People with chronic kidney or <span class="qt0">liver</span> disease, which can affect your ability to change vitamin D into a form your body can use.</li><li>People who take medicines that affect vitamin D levels, including certain cholesterol, anti-seizure, steroid, and weight-loss medicines.</li></ul><p>Talk with your provider if you are at risk for vitamin D deficiency.  There is a blood test that can measure how much vitamin D is in your body.</p>What problems does vitamin D deficiency cause?<p>Vitamin D deficiency can lead to a loss of bone density, which can contribute to osteoporosis and fractures (broken bones).</p><p>Severe vitamin D deficiency can also lead to other diseases:</p><ul><li>In children, it can cause rickets. Rickets is a rare disease that causes the bones to become soft and bend. African American infants and children are at higher risk of getting rickets.</li><li>In <span class="qt3">adults</span>, severe vitamin D deficiency leads to osteomalacia. Osteomalacia causes weak bones, bone pain, and muscle weakness.</li></ul>How can I get more vitamin D?<p>There are a few foods that naturally have some vitamin D:</p><ul><li>Fatty fish such as salmon, tuna, and mackerel</li><li>Beef <span class="qt0">liver</span></li><li>Cheese</li><li>Mushrooms</li><li>Egg yolks</li></ul><p>You can also get vitamin D from fortified foods. You can check the food labels to find out whether a food has vitamin D. Foods that often have added vitamin D include:</p><ul><li>Milk</li><li>Breakfast cereals</li><li>Orange juice</li><li>Other dairy products, such as yogurt</li><li>Soy drinks</li></ul><p>Vitamin D is in many multivitamins. There are also vitamin D supplements, both in pills and in a liquid for babies.</p><p>If you have vitamin D deficiency, the treatment is with supplements. Check with your provider about how much you need to take, how often you need to take it, and how long you need to take it.</p>Can too much vitamin D be harmful?<p>Getting too much vitamin D (known as vitamin D toxicity) can be harmful. Signs of toxicity include nausea and vomiting, poor appetite, constipation, weakness, and weight loss.</p><p>Very high levels of vitamin D can damage the kidneys. It also raises the level of calcium in your blood. High levels of blood calcium (hypercalcemia) can cause confusion, kidney failure, and irregular heartbeat (arrhythmia).</p><p>Most cases of vitamin D toxicity happen when someone overuses vitamin D supplements. You cannot get too much vitamin D from sun exposure because the skin limits the amount of vitamin D it makes.</p></content>
